source: Ilic & Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in LLMs
finding: Test scores of LLMs show a positive manifold. Every pair of the 12 tests correlates positively, like human ability tests.
numbers: 591 LLMs after de-duplication (from 3862 scraped; 2415 and 1599 subsamples gave similar results). 12 tests aligned to Gf, Gkn, Grw, Gq. Mean inter-test r = 0.73 (range 0.35 to 0.99). KMO 0.93.
limits: Models are not independent draws (fine-tunes of shared bases). Correlations among Gkn tests were 0.98-0.99, so part of the manifold is shared test method. Open LLM Leaderboard tests only.
agent_relevance: Supports treating 'how strong is the base model' as one dominant dimension; scaffold gains should be judged against that baseline.

source: Ilic & Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in LLMs
finding: A second-order general factor fits. It explains far more variance than the human g.
numbers: General factor explains 65.6% of variance (7.87/12), mean g loading 0.81 (range 0.64-0.96), omega hierarchical 0.94. Human g typically 40-50% (Deary 2009). Highest g loading: maths composite (0.96). Mean inter-test r on the six short tests: 0.63 (human 0.45-0.50).
limits: RMSEA above 0.08 (authors lean on SRMR 0.025). Variance is between models, not within a person, so not directly comparable with human data.
agent_relevance: Between-model differences are mostly one axis. A per-problem-class routing signal from broad abilities may add little over overall model strength.

source: Ilic & Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in LLMs
finding: Only one merged knowledge and reading/writing group factor appeared, not four separate CHC broad factors (Gf, Gkn, Grw, Gq).
numbers: Final structure: g plus a combined Gkn/Grw group factor. Gq and Gf did not separate as group factors.
limits: Only four broad abilities measurable from leaderboard tests; no speed, memory or visual tests.
agent_relevance: The human nine-broad-ability vocabulary does not transfer one to one to LLMs; use it as a loose problem-class naming scheme only.

source: Ilic & Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in LLMs
finding: Parameter count predicts the general factor, with strong diminishing returns.
numbers: Pearson r = 0.54 (95% CI 0.48-0.59), Spearman 0.62 between parameters and general factor score (n = 579). Cubic spline beat linear: F(2,573)=27.93, eta2 = 0.063. Fast gains from 0.1B to about 10B, plateau 10-20B, slow rise to 80B. Gkn/Grw factor: Pearson r = 0.11, Spearman 0.42; no association beyond 45B.
limits: Only 10 models above 80B. Parameter count is confounded with training data and family.
agent_relevance: Size alone is not the lever above mid-size; scaffold design is a separate lever.

source: Ilic & Gignac (2024) Evidence of interrelated cognitive-like capabilities in LLMs
finding: Authors say LLM g may reflect achievement or expertise rather than intelligence, because the tests are mostly knowledge and trained skills.
numbers: Title and abstract: 'whether LLMs manifest primarily achievement/expertise rather than intelligence remains to be determined'.
limits: Interpretation, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: Do not read a high g as flexible reasoning; test on novel items.

source: Burnell et al. (2023) Revealing the structure of language model capabilities
finding: Factor analysis of HELM data found three factors, not one: reasoning, comprehension, core language modelling.
numbers: 29 LLMs x 27 tasks. Hull method picked 3 factors; oblimin EFA explained 0.33, 0.31, 0.17 (cumulative 0.82). Bayesian factor analysis gave a matching 3-factor solution (LSAT was the one task left unassigned).
limits: Tiny sample (29 models) so frequentist fit was poor: CFI 0.70, TLI 0.61, RMSEA 0.26. Factor labels set by one expert annotator.
agent_relevance: Gives a data-driven set of problem classes (reasoning, comprehension, LM) rather than human CHC labels.

source: Burnell et al. (2023) Revealing the structure of language model capabilities
finding: The three LLM factors are only moderately correlated (a weak g-like overlap) and relate differently to model properties.
numbers: Factor correlations about 0.43-0.51 (CIs wide, e.g. 0.19 to 0.73). Log model size vs comprehension r = 0.70 [0.46, 0.85]; vs language modelling r = -0.50 [-0.72, -0.17]; vs reasoning r = 0.08 [-0.38, 0.52]. Instruction tuning: negative with language modelling, positive with reasoning, near zero with comprehension.
limits: CIs wide. Training tokens varied little so no conclusion on data size. HELM tasks from 2022 era.
agent_relevance: Instruction tuning raised the reasoning factor and lowered the raw LM factor: abilities can move opposite ways, so one score hides trade-offs.

source: Burnell et al. (2023) Revealing the structure of language model capabilities
finding: Deductive tasks (bAbI, Dyck) loaded only weakly on the reasoning factor; bias tests (BBQ, TruthfulQA) loaded strongly on it.
numbers: GSM8K loaded strongly on reasoning; HellaSwag commonsense loaded on comprehension.
limits: Interpretation by one annotator.
agent_relevance: Task labels like 'reasoning' are unreliable; classify problems by empirical co-variation.

source: Ruan, Maddison & Hashimoto (2024) Observational Scaling Laws and the Predictability of Language Model Performance
finding: One principal component of benchmark scores carries most of the variance in LM ability, with two more interpretable ones.
numbers: 77 open LMs from 21 families. PC-1 explains about 80% of variance, top 3 PCs about 97%. PC-1 = general capability (weighted average of all metrics), PC-2 = reasoning (maths, coding), PC-3 = programming.
limits: PCA, not factor analysis; benchmark set is fixed.
agent_relevance: Low-dimensional capability space: a general axis plus reasoning and code. Matches a coarse split of problem classes.

source: Ruan, Maddison & Hashimoto (2024) Observational Scaling Laws and the Predictability of Language Model Performance
finding: PC measures scale log-linearly with compute inside each family (R2 > 0.9) and let weak models predict GPT-4-class results, including agent benchmarks.
numbers: PCs linearly correlated with log-compute within families, R2 > 0.9. Prediction of GPT-4 and Claude-2 level performance from models weaker than GPT-3.5 shown for AgentBench and AgentBoard. PC-1 spans at least 5 orders of magnitude, unlike saturating single benchmarks (HellaSwag, WinoGrande) or floor-limited ones (MMLU, GSM8K for small models).
limits: Post-training techniques such as chain-of-thought are a stated open area.
agent_relevance: A general factor score is a smoother measure than single benchmarks; useful for measuring scaffold gain on one scale.

source: Kipnis et al. (2025) metabench: a sparse benchmark of reasoning and knowledge
finding: Six benchmarks share one general ability among LLMs.
numbers: n > 5000 LLMs, six benchmarks (ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande; 28,632 items). A single factor on benchmark-specific IRT abilities captures 79.3% of variability and correlates r = 0.938 with the grand mean; loadings 0.771 (GSM8K) to 0.966 (WinoGrande).
limits: Six knowledge and reasoning benchmarks only; no speed, memory or visual tests.
agent_relevance: Supports one overall strength axis among models.

source: Kipnis et al. (2025) metabench: a sparse benchmark of reasoning and knowledge
finding: Items are highly redundant: under 3% of items rebuild scores.
numbers: Under 3% of original size; reconstructs each benchmark score with 1.24% RMSE on average and the total score with 0.58% RMSE. Estimated latent abilities carry information beyond sum scores.
limits: Reconstruction tested by cross-validation on open-leaderboard models.
agent_relevance: If few items measure the factor, cheap probes could classify a problem's demands before spending budget.

source: Maia Polo et al. (2024) tinyBenchmarks: evaluating LLMs with fewer examples
finding: IRT-based item selection estimates full benchmark scores from 100 examples.
numbers: 100 curated examples per scenario give about 2% average performance estimation error across the benchmarks tested.
limits: Mostly leaderboard-style benchmarks; shift to new models matters.
agent_relevance: Same point as metabench: small item sets place a model on the ability scale.

source: Maia Polo et al. (2024/2025) Sloth: scaling laws for LLM skills
finding: A latent-skills scaling law (reasoning, instruction following etc.) predicts benchmark scores across model families.
numbers: 12 benchmarks from Open LLM Leaderboard v1/v2. Sloth gets errors similar to or lower than a 'size and tokens' scaling law without training several model sizes per family. Its related-work section restates Ilic's g, Burnell's three factors and Kipnis's 80% main factor.
limits: Mean absolute error measured within family; number of skills chosen by the authors.
agent_relevance: Skills treated as low-dimensional latents that compute raises; paper also models test-time compute.

source: Hendrycks et al. (2025) A Definition of AGI
finding: First direct use of CHC broad abilities as an AI yardstick: ten equal-weighted components, 10% each.
numbers: Components: general knowledge K, reading/writing RW, maths M, on-the-spot reasoning R, working memory WM, long-term memory storage MS, retrieval MR, visual V, auditory A, speed S. AGI score: GPT-4 (2023) 27%, GPT-5 (2025) 57%.
limits: Authors' own task battery and scoring; equal weights are a design choice; not a psychometric fit.
agent_relevance: Gives problem-class vocabulary straight from CHC. Weak classes (MS, V, WM) show where an agent needs external scaffolds.

source: Hendrycks et al. (2025) A Definition of AGI
finding: Profile is jagged: strong in knowledge, reading, maths; near zero in long-term memory storage.
numbers: Points per component, GPT-4 then GPT-5: K 8/9, RW 6/10, M 4/10, R 0/7, WM 2/4, MS 0/0, MR 4/4, V 0/4, A 0/6, S 3/3. Authors call long-term memory storage the main bottleneck.
limits: Single paper, two models, own scoring.
agent_relevance: The schema must supply memory from outside; visual reasoning is another weak class.

source: Hendrycks et al. (2025) A Definition of AGI
finding: Warns of 'capability contortions': strengths used to compensate for weaknesses, creating an illusion of generality.
numbers: Stated in the paper's discussion section.
limits: Qualitative claim.
agent_relevance: A scaffold is partly such a contortion; evaluate on held-out cases so reports say what is external.

source: Zhuang et al. (2023/2025) AI evaluation should learn from how we test humans (adaptive testing)
finding: Position paper: LLM evaluation should use psychometric adaptive testing built on IRT; it names Spearman's g and CHC as the model of general intelligence.
numbers: No new factor fit. Argues accuracy such as GPT-4o 85.7% on a medical QA set is hard to interpret without item-level ability estimates.
limits: Position paper; few new measurements.
agent_relevance: Use item-level tests rather than raw accuracy when judging scaffold gains.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Evaluating General-Purpose AI with Psychometrics
finding: Proposes construct-oriented evaluation: latent constructs rather than single tasks, with warnings about pitfalls.
numbers: Cites the 29-LLM, 27-task factor analysis as evidence that structure exists. Framework paper, no new factor fit.
limits: No empirical factor study.
agent_relevance: Background for building a problem-class taxonomy.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat humans on a Raven-style text matrix task (a classic Gf paradigm).
numbers: Digit Matrices, humans N = 40 undergraduates. Generative: GPT-3 above human mean, odds ratio 1.88 (95% CI 1.21-2.91), p = 0.005. Multiple choice: OR 6.27 (CI 3.28-11.99). Best human answered everything correctly. Human-model difficulty profile correlated r(30) = 0.39, p = 0.027.
limits: New text format may differ from visual Raven; contamination argued against but not excluded; GPT-3 only.
agent_relevance: Gf tasks in text format are not a safe sign of fluid reasoning; check on novel formats.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: On letter-string analogies GPT-3 beat humans at zero generalizations, and degraded with more generalizations like humans did.
numbers: Humans N=57 UCLA undergraduates. Zero-generalization problems: OR 1.76 (CI 1.27-2.46), p = 0.0007. Other tasks: verbal analogies N=57, story analogies N=54.
limits: Items designed by the authors; later counterfactual-variant studies reported failures (not opened here).
agent_relevance: Matches a single Gf-like capacity, but robustness to variants is the real test.

source: Moskvichev, Odouard & Mitchell (2023) The ConceptARC Benchmark
finding: Humans far beat machine solvers on a concept-grouped ARC benchmark (abstraction, a Gf paradigm).
numbers: 16 concept groups x 10 tasks x 3 test inputs; three guesses allowed. Humans about 84% per task, over 90% on 11 of 16 concepts and over 80% on the other 5. Kaggle ARC first place 21%, second 19% on hidden ARC (ensemble about 31%); on ConceptARC first place averaged 40 points below humans. Text-only GPT-4 did worst, e.g. Count 0.03 and Copy 0.07 versus 0.86 and 0.93 for humans.
limits: GPT-4 was language-only with a text-grid prompt; 2023 model.
agent_relevance: Fluid abstraction is the clearest class where plain LLMs fail; the natural target for scaffolding.

source: Gendron et al. (2023) Large Language Models Are Not Strong Abstract Reasoners
finding: Open-ended abstract reasoning (including RAVEN-text) stays poor, and chain-of-thought did not help overall.
numbers: RAVENT open QA accuracy (text, symbolic): GPT-4 0.410 and 0.330, Text-Davinci-3 0.343 and 0.234, GPT-3.5-Turbo 0.226 and 0.161, LLaMA-7B 0.000. ARCT: GPT-4 0.119. CoT results 'not higher' than base; multiple-choice RAVENT scores fell for all models with CoT; GPT-3.5 rose on PVR and RAVENT open QA. Fine-tuned LLaMA2 near-perfect in distribution but only partly transferred to alternate syntax.
limits: 2023 models; text conversion of RAVEN; authors blame faithful reasoning, not prompt quality.
agent_relevance: Prompt style alone does not repair Gf-type tasks; do not expect gain from 'think step by step'.

source: Chollet (2019) On the Measure of Intelligence
finding: Ties the CHC hierarchy to generalization levels: local, broad and extreme generalization correspond to narrow abilities, broad abilities and g.
numbers: Text states CHC has three strata (g, broad, narrow) and that 'extreme generalization' corresponds to g. Introduces ARC as a skill-acquisition test.
limits: Conceptual paper, no factor data.
agent_relevance: Bridge from psychometric strata to testing agents on unseen tasks.

source: Owen (2024) How predictable is language model benchmark performance?
finding: Aggregate benchmark performance is decently predictable from compute; single tasks are not.
numbers: Five orders of magnitude of compute, eleven architectures. BIG-Bench Hard extrapolated one order of magnitude: 6 points average absolute error; individual BIG-Bench tasks 18 points.
limits: Averaging hides task-level jaggedness.
agent_relevance: General score is stable; per-task results are noisy, so classes should be estimated from many items.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) General Scales Unlock AI Evaluation (ADeLe)
finding: Builds 18 demand scales (11 cognitive capabilities, 5 knowledge dimensions, extraneous ones) to label each item and predict LLM success.
numbers: 15 LLMs, 63 tasks. Demand-level assessor: weighted AUROC 0.81 (ECE 0.02) in distribution; LLaMA-embedding 0.79 and GloVe 0.74 baselines. Out of distribution: weighted AUROC 0.75, ECE 0.04. GPT-4o as subject: 0.88. Annotation agreement with GPT-4o: rWG above 0.75 on every dimension (mean 0.86).
limits: Annotations produced by an LLM annotator; dimensions chosen by authors, not derived from factor analysis.
agent_relevance: Closest existing problem-class vocabulary from a psychometric stance; per-item demand labels predict failure better than embeddings.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) General Scales Unlock AI Evaluation (ADeLe)
finding: Ability profiles: knowledge dimensions follow model size; quantitative, logical, abstraction and social reasoning are boosted by chain-of-thought or inference-heavy models.
numbers: Three LLM families compared; o1 and R1-Distill raise reasoning-type abilities. Dimensions moderately correlated, consistent with a hierarchy. ADeLe-Light subset reproduces results.
limits: Few families.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-time compute helps class by class: reasoning yes, knowledge no.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) General Scales Unlock AI Evaluation (ADeLe)
finding: Many benchmarks do not measure what they say: they carry demands on extraneous dimensions (atypicality, volume, unguessability).
numbers: Authors read these as signs of contamination, amalgamation or funnelling (Table 14 in the paper). Many benchmarks lack specificity or sensitivity for the dimension their designers claimed.
limits: Based on their rubrics.
agent_relevance: Check that a probe measures the intended class before using it as a router.
